subject: giraffe
pitch: A young reticulated giraffe. Chestnut patches outlined by bright cream lines all over its body and neck, a short mane of stiff brown hair down the neck, two fuzzy ossicones with black tufts on top, big ears, long lashes, a long dark tongue just peeking out, and slender legs fading to cream above the hooves.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a single TypeScript module for a giraffe model using the SDK, focusing on getting realistic proportions right—young giraffe height, body length, and leg height—while keeping the API usage safe and testable-free robust.

Now I'm sketching out the skeleton layout: hip and spine joints positioned along the body, a catmull spine chain connecting hips to withers, and planning how the neck and head joints attach, making sure parent-child joint relationships and chain naming stay consistent.

For the head, I'm placing a downward-tilted muzzle frustum, a blocky skull, ossicone spikes with dark tufts on top, and side-mounted ears built from an extruded outline positioned in the forward-up plane with thickness extending sideways.

Now I'm thinking through eyes as dark spheres with lash rings, and realizing it's simpler to just use model-space coordinates directly rather than fighting with the head bone's tilted local frame.

For the tongue, I'll add a capsule shape tapering from the mouth down and forward, binding it explicitly to the head bone so it tracks correctly. For the giraffe-style coat, I'm considering using an irregular patch pattern with cream lines separating chestnut patches.

For the legs, I want them to fade from chestnut above into cream near the hooves, so I'm using a gradient paint between those two points, possibly nesting the patch pattern inside the gradient for the upper leg. For the mane, I'm thinking of scattering short stiff hair cards along a neck sweep surface rather than placing them individually.

Actually, for mane strands, spikes along the dorsal line of the neck sweep seem simpler—using an "along" helper to place small colored spikes at intervals following the neck curve. For the body, I'm planning a sweep along a spine path built from catmull-rom control points, with radius varying by position and bound to the spine bone chain.

For the body I'll use a sweep directly over the spine chain as the source, letting it skin automatically with a radius function returning elliptical dimensions that widen through the barrel and round off at the rump. For the neck, I'll taper the radius from thick at the base to thin near the head using a linear falloff function along the chain.

Now I'm working out leg placement and reach: setting hip anchors for front and hind legs, then checking whether the limb segment lengths can actually span from hip height down to the ground where the hooves need to land. I'm adjusting hip height and segment lengths since my first attempt put the foot target out of reach, so I'm recalculating to keep the leg within its max extension.

With that sorted, I'm defining the leg chains—shoulder/knee/ankle joints for front legs, with forward bends for the knee and backward bends for the hind hock—and figuring out how many names correspond to how many joints in the chain so the hoof ends up at the right tip position.

Now I'm working out how to attach each leg chain to the right parent spine joint (chest area for front legs, hips for hind), and planning how to sweep the leg geometry with a tapering radius and a separate hoof piece at the foot tip.

For the hooves, I'm placing a small cylinder at each leg's end joint, positioned so it rests flush on the ground. I'm also figuring out the gradient paint on the legs, blending cream near the top to a deeper tone further down, and starting to think through how that connects to the body's patch coloring.

Now I'm moving to the tail: a thin tapering sweep curving down from the hips with a dark sphere tuft at the tip, then the ossicones on top of the head — short capsule shapes with a dark knob — and finally the ears, which I'll build using an extruded outline shape positioned and oriented against the head.

For the mane, I'm walking along the neck's center line and placing spike shapes pointing dorsally upward at regular intervals to create a row of stiff brown hair.

Now I'm settling on the color palette — cream base, chestnut patches, dark brown mane, near-black hooves and nose — and planning to use a patches-style paint function to scatter chestnut markings across the cream base coat on the head and body geometry.

Working out the body and neck paint using patches with a set size, gap, and seed so the pattern reads as continuous across the surfaces, then figuring out how to fade the leg coloring from cream at the top to the body pattern lower down using a gradient function anchored to points along each leg's position.

For the eyelashes, I'm arranging them in a ring around the eye's vertical axis with an angular range covering the front arc, tilted upward so they fan outward from the front of each side-facing eye—a reasonable approximation given giraffe eyes sit on the sides of the head.

Now I'm working through the head geometry: placing the skull as a box, the muzzle as a tapered frustum shape, ossicones as capsules with small dark tufts on top, and eyes as dark spheres bulging out near the skull's sides, all positioned relative to the head bone joint.

I'm placing the tongue as a small capsule peeking out past the muzzle's tip, and defining the ears as extruded outline shapes in the z-y plane set to the sides of the head, giving them a flat, forward-backward spread with thickness and beveled edges.

Rethinking the ear orientation, I realize real giraffe ears sit flat and horizontal, sticking out sideways rather than vertically, so I'm reworking the extrusion axes so the outline sits in the z-x plane with vertical thickness, letting the ear project outward along the mirrored x-axis for each side.

Adjusting body proportions and spine path...

Now I'm chaining the neck onto the spine's last joint, with the head attached at the neck's end point, keeping radii tapering from base to tip. Then I'm setting up leg roots under the shoulders and hips, figuring out foot target positions for the front legs under the chest.

Still working out leg lengths...

Still defining leg naming and sweep gradients...

Now I'm working out the hoof cylinders attached to chain tips, then moving to the tail chain built from a catmull curve with tapering radius and a tuft at the end, figuring out how to reference the tail's tip joint given auto-generated names.

I'm now sketching the full giraffe build function—defining color palette, joints for hips, spine, neck, head, and tail chains, sweeping bodies with gradient/patch coloring, looping over left/right legs for front and hind limbs with inverse-kinematic chains and hoof parts, and planning ear extrusions and eye/mane details using ring and spike helpers.

I'm detailing the head features: eyes with lash rings, ossicones capped with fuzzy dark tufts, a boxy skull, a frustum-shaped muzzle, a dark nose, and a small tongue capsule peeking past the muzzle.
